title: The Popsicle and the forgotten drink
hook: A boy left a drink outside on a cold night and woke up to a frozen treat.
peek: The story goes that in 1905 an 11-year-old in the San Francisco Bay Area left a cup of fruit drink outside with the stirring stick still in it. Nearly twenty years later, he patented the result.
lede: Frank Epperson told the story for the rest of his life. As a boy of 11 in 1905, he mixed a fruity soda drink from powder and water, left it on the porch with a wooden stirrer in the cup, and forgot about it. A cold night froze it solid around the stick. In the morning he pulled it out and had an ice pop.

bullets.text: The tale has only one source: Epperson himself. Hard frosts are rare around San Francisco Bay, so some writers doubt the details. It may well be true, but nobody else recorded it happening.
Epperson waited until the early 1920s to sell his ice pops, at an amusement park in Alameda, California. In 1923 he applied for a patent on frozen treats on a stick, which he called the Epsicle.

His own children reportedly called it Pop's 'sicle, after their father, and that name stuck instead. Within a couple of years Epperson sold the rights to the Joe Lowe Company of New York, which made Popsicle a national brand.
During the Great Depression the company brought out a pop with two sticks. Two children could snap it in half and share one treat bought for a single nickel.
